strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck for diffusion policies: multi-step denoising latency in closed-loop robotic control. The proposed rollout-adaptive pruning/caching framing is well motivated by the observation that fixed schedules vary in quality across rollout iterations.

The method is technically coherent: an observation-conditioned pruner predicts a global mask over denoising steps and DiT blocks, a sparsity loss enforces a compute budget, and the one-for-all cache reuse strategy targets both cross-timestep and cross-block redundancy.

The empirical evaluation is broad for a robotics acceleration paper, covering RoboMimic PH/MH tasks, Franka Kitchen, and a real-world pick-and-release setup. Across tables, SAG generally improves the speed/accuracy tradeoff over DDIM, EfficientVLA, BAC, Falcon, SDP, CP, and L2C.
Ablations support the main design choices: removing the real-time pruner, one-for-all reuse, or global sparsity loss reduces success substantially, especially for high sparsity settings.

The paper includes useful implementation details, pretrained checkpoint sources, pruning-rate plots, training curves, latency tables, and a statement on LLM use, which helps assess reproducibility and research ethics.
weaknesses: The central claim of “lossless” acceleration is overstated. SAG sometimes slightly underperforms full precision, e.g. Can PH 98 vs 99, Tool PH 50 vs 51, Transport MH 50 vs 54, while also sometimes improving success. These differences may be within variance, but the paper should avoid categorical lossless claims or provide statistical tests.

The pruner requires task-specific training data and extra training, but this cost and deployment assumption are not fully analyzed. The method is less training-free than parts of the framing suggest, and it is unclear how well the pruner transfers across policies, tasks, cameras, domains, or distribution shifts.

The real-world evidence is limited: only one pick-and-release task is reported, with low absolute success rates even for SAG at 54%. This supports promise but not strong claims about real-time robotic reliability.

Some experimental reporting is confusing or inconsistent. The project page field is blank, Table 5 averages appear inconsistent with the listed task latencies, and the text says “45.1%” inference frequency while Figure 5 appears to show 40.5 Hz. These issues reduce confidence in reproducibility and presentation polish.

The baseline comparison may not be fully normalized. Methods differ in whether they require distillation, different denoising steps, task-specific tuning, or different compression objectives, and the paper gives limited detail on hyperparameter selection and fairness beyond a few settings.

The methodology leaves some technical ambiguities: the shared cache buffer across blocks of the same type may reuse activations with different layer distributions, but the paper does not deeply analyze failure modes, cache initialization effects, or why the resulting residual substitution remains stable under very high pruning.

The limitations discussion is weak. The manuscript does not adequately discuss dependence on simulation benchmarks, possible safety risks from stale cached activations in closed-loop control, degradation under out-of-distribution observations, or computational/training overhead beyond inference FLOPs.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck: multi-step diffusion policies are too slow for high-frequency visuomotor control, and adaptive activation reuse is a relevant direction.

The proposed combination of an observation-conditioned pruning mask, a global sparsity constraint, and cross-block/cross-timestep activation reuse is conceptually plausible and more adaptive than fixed caching schedules.

The evaluation covers several standard simulated manipulation benchmarks and compares against multiple acceleration baselines, with reported speedups around 3.6-4x and generally preserved simulated success rates.
The paper includes useful ablations for the real-time pruner, one-for-all reuse, global sparsity loss, positional encoding, and target pruning behavior.
weaknesses: The central evidence is not sufficiently convincing for the strong claims of 'lossless' acceleration. Several reported SAG success rates are only similar to full precision within variance, sometimes lower, and the real-world success rate is only 54%, which is presented positively despite being poor for deployment.

The learned pruner is trained on task-specific reference data and uses expert-action fidelity, but the paper repeatedly frames the approach as acceleration without updating model parameters. This is misleading: the policy is frozen, but an additional trained model is required per task, with nontrivial data and training assumptions.

The methodology is underspecified in critical ways. The exact cached activation semantics, initialization effects, compatibility across different block types, dimensional handling for cross-block reuse, and how reuse errors propagate through residual streams are not explained rigorously enough to reproduce or trust the mechanism.

The motivation for rollout adaptivity is weakly established. Figure 1 uses only three randomly generated schedules on one task and a leave-one-rollout-step protocol that is not clearly tied to actual deployed fixed schedules; this is too thin to justify the broad claim that static schedules fundamentally fail.

Baseline comparison fairness is unclear. Hyperparameters for several baselines appear fixed from prior work or chosen ad hoc, while SAG receives task-specific pruner training. There is no clear compute-normalized or tuning-normalized comparison, and some baselines are adapted from other domains without enough detail.

The reported 'average performance gain' claims are confusing because SAG sometimes exceeds the full-precision policy, which suggests evaluation noise or changed stochasticity rather than genuine acceleration quality. The paper does not analyze statistical significance, number of trials per seed, or why a pruned/reused policy should outperform the teacher.

Ablations are not fully isolating. For example, replacing the real-time pruner with a fixed schedule generated by the pruner does not clearly test adaptivity against a well-optimized fixed schedule; replacing global sparsity loss causes catastrophic failures, but the alternative is not sufficiently tuned to make the conclusion robust.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper mentions a project page but provides no concrete code release details, incomplete checkpoint links in the appendix, limited implementation details for the baselines, and insufficient information about evaluation protocols and real-world trials.

The paper lacks a serious limitations and ethics discussion. Safety implications of approximate action generation in closed-loop robot control, failure modes under distribution shift, and real-world deployment risks are not treated adequately.

Presentation has several issues: overclaiming, inconsistent terminology around pruning/caching/reuse, equations and algorithms that do not fully match the described architecture, and some awkward or imprecise writing that makes the technical contribution harder to audit.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck for diffusion policies: multi-step denoising latency in closed-loop robot control. The proposed observation-conditioned pruning mask and one-for-all activation reuse are well motivated by rollout-dependent sparsity and cross-block/timestep redundancy.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this topic, covering RoboMimic PH/MH tasks, Kitchen, several acceleration baselines, ablations, latency measurements, and a real-world pick-and-release experiment. SAG generally achieves a strong accuracy/speed tradeoff, e.g. about 3.6-4.0x speedups while maintaining or slightly improving success rates on many simulation tasks.

The ablations support the main design choices: removing the adaptive pruner, one-for-all reuse, or global sparsity loss causes meaningful drops, with the global sparsity loss especially important under high pruning.
The method is useful because it can accelerate pretrained diffusion policies without updating the policy parameters, which makes it potentially easy to deploy on existing DP-T checkpoints.
weaknesses: Some central claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly claims lossless acceleration, but SAG is not uniformly lossless: for example Can-PH drops from 99 to 98, Tool-PH from 51 to 50, and Transport-MH from 54 to 50, while standard deviations overlap. The results are strong, but the wording should be more careful.

The real-world evidence is limited and not fully specified. The pick-and-release experiment reports only 54% success for SAG, and the manuscript does not state the number of trials, confidence intervals, failure modes, or whether policies/baselines were equally tuned. This weakens claims about robust real-time deployment.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives useful hyperparameters and checkpoint sources, but the project page appears blank in the manuscript, and it is unclear whether code, trained pruners, exact evaluation scripts, random seeds, trial counts, and baseline adaptation details will be released.

The method requires task-specific pruner training using reference data, which makes it less training-free than some baselines and may limit transfer to new embodiments, observation distributions, or substantially different policies. This cost and its scaling are not analyzed deeply.

The comparison to baselines would benefit from more careful normalization of speed/quality tradeoffs. Some baselines such as DDIM have similar speed and comparable success on several tasks, while CP is much faster but lower quality; plotting Pareto curves over multiple sparsity/pruning or denoising settings would make the advantage more convincing.

There is no substantial limitations or ethics discussion beyond LLM usage. For a robotics acceleration paper, the authors should discuss safety risks from pruning-induced action errors, out-of-distribution observations, and deployment safeguards.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck for diffusion policies: multi-step denoising latency in closed-loop robot control. The proposed observation-conditioned pruning schedule is well motivated by the rollout-dependent behavior shown in the leave-one-out schedule analysis.

The method is technically plausible and combines several useful ingredients: a lightweight pruner predicting a global timestep-by-block mask, an explicit sparsity budget loss, and cross-timestep/cross-block activation reuse. The ablations support the importance of these components, especially global allocation and one-for-all reuse.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this area, covering RoboMimic PH/MH tasks, Kitchen, sampler compatibility, pruning-rate sensitivity, robustness tests, and some real-robot experiments. Across these settings SAG generally preserves full-computation success rates while improving latency by about 3.5-4x.

The appendix provides helpful reproducibility details, including hardware, training hyperparameters, reference-set sizes, pruning-rate behavior, latency tables, and additional sparsity visualizations. The limitations section is honest about scope and deployment generality.
weaknesses: The central claim of rollout-adaptive pruning is only partially established. The learned pruner is trained from task-specific reference data and evaluated mostly on the same task distribution, so it is unclear whether it has learned broadly useful rollout adaptivity rather than task-specific mask patterns. There is no cross-task, cross-environment, or held-out-condition generalization study of the pruner itself.

The training objective uses expert ground-truth actions rather than matching the original diffusion policy distribution, and SAG sometimes outperforms full computation. This makes the comparison ambiguous: the method is presented as acceleration without changing policy behavior, but the pruner training can effectively alter behavior through the induced sparse computation path.

The real-world evidence is promising but not strong enough for the broad real-time deployment claims. The paper reports three tasks and frequencies, but the main real-world table does not clearly state trial counts or statistical uncertainty; one task has low absolute success for both full computation and SAG, and robustness results show complete failure under low light.

Some baseline comparisons may be fragile. Consistency Policy is much faster but performs poorly under the chosen setting, while the appendix's compute-matched comparison reports surprisingly weak CP performance even with larger budgets. More careful tuning and matched wall-clock comparisons would be needed to rule out baseline under-optimization.

The reported speedups are useful but less dramatic than the pruning rate might suggest: over 90% pruning translates to roughly 3.6-4x speedup, and SAG is slower than CP. The paper should more clearly separate theoretical sparsity, wall-clock latency, and practical control frequency.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are notable issues: some tables/claims use averages that are hard to reconcile with the displayed numbers, several references and project links appear placeholder-like or incomplete, and the method description leaves implementation details of cache initialization, mask grouping, and pruner overhead insufficiently precise for exact reproduction.

Ethics and safety considerations are thin for a real-robot acceleration method. Faster but approximate action generation can introduce control instability or unsafe failures, yet the paper mainly discusses benchmark success rates and gives little guidance on safety monitoring, fallback to full computation, or deployment constraints.

strengths: The problem is practically important: diffusion-policy inference latency is a real bottleneck for closed-loop robotic control, and the paper targets an impactful efficiency-performance tradeoff.

The proposed combination of an observation-conditioned pruning mask, global sparsity budget, and cross-block/timestep activation reuse is a plausible and reasonably original extension of caching/pruning ideas to action diffusion.

The empirical section is broad on paper: RoboMimic PH/MH tasks, Franka Kitchen, several acceleration baselines, ablations, pruning-rate sensitivity, DPM-Solver compatibility, latency tables, robustness checks, and a small real-robot evaluation are included.

Some reported results are promising, especially the roughly 3.6-4.0x simulation speedups with comparable success rates on many tasks and the improvement on the real-world assembly-line task relative to full computation.
weaknesses: The central claims are not sufficiently well supported. The motivation for rollout-adaptive schedules rests heavily on a leave-one-out experiment with only three randomly generated fixed schedules; this does not rule out strong learned/static schedules or better-tuned per-task schedules, so the evidence for the core adaptivity claim is weak.

The method and evaluation leave important ambiguities. It is unclear whether separate pruners are trained per task, how much task-specific tuning is used, how baselines are tuned to comparable budgets, whether action-generation latency includes observation encoding/pruner overhead consistently, and whether all baselines use equally optimized implementations.

Several results are internally inconsistent or overstated. The paper claims real-time robot-control suitability, but the real-world SAG frequencies are 44.3-46.1 Hz, below the paper's own stated 50-1000 Hz Franka requirement. The introduction's 50 ms/20 Hz example also conflicts with later simulation latencies around 1.55 s for full computation. Claims of average performance gains are also hard to reconcile with tables where SAG is often comparable to or below full computation.

The real-world evidence is too small and uneven for the strength of the claims. Only three tasks are reported, with unclear trial counts in the main table, and SAG reduces Stack Bowls success from 82% to 78% while improving Assembly Line. This supports possible usefulness, not broad real-world reliability.

The training objective uses imitation loss to ground-truth actions from a reference subset rather than directly preserving the full policy distribution or task return, but the paper does not analyze when this surrogate is valid. At 97% pruning performance collapses on several tasks, suggesting the approach has sharp failure modes that deserve deeper analysis.

The one-for-all reuse mechanism is underspecified and potentially fragile: reusing a single shared activation buffer across blocks of the same type assumes strong cross-block compatibility, but the paper mainly provides similarity visualizations rather than a rigorous account of when dimensions, normalization, and residual semantics make this safe.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. The project-page field is blank, code is not provided, many implementation choices are omitted or scattered, and the real-world data/protocols are not described in enough detail to reproduce. The appendix gives some hyperparameters but not enough to rebuild the full system and baseline comparisons reliably.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. There are many spacing/formatting issues, awkward claims, table inconsistencies, a reference with 'Placeholder Publisher' and another saying 'Submitted to Some Conference', and some captions/sections appear hastily prepared.

The ethics/impact statement is inaccurate: it says no new human subjects or personal data were involved and that all experiments use public simulation datasets, but the main text reports collecting 200 real-world teleoperation demonstrations per task. Even if low risk, this contradiction undermines confidence in the paper's treatment of research ethics and data provenance.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important bottleneck for diffusion policies: multi-step denoising is often too slow for closed-loop robotic control. The proposed combination of an observation-conditioned pruning mask and cross-step/cross-block activation reuse is well motivated by rollout dynamics and activation redundancy.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area. The paper reports results on RoboMimic PH/MH, Franka Kitchen, and three real-world Franka tasks, with comparisons to full computation, DDIM, EfficientVLA, L2C, BAC, Falcon, SDP, and Consistency Policy. SAG generally preserves or slightly improves success rates while achieving about 3.6-4.0x speedup, which is a meaningful practical gain.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices. Removing the real-time pruner, one-for-all reuse, or global sparsity loss causes notable drops in average success, suggesting the gains are not due to a single incidental implementation choice.

The method is compatible with sampler-level acceleration, and the compute-matched comparison with Consistency Policy helps address the concern that SAG is merely equivalent to shortening the denoising trajectory.

The limitations and impact sections are present and mostly appropriate: the authors acknowledge restricted policy families, platforms, tasks, fixed compute budget, and the need for representative reference data. No major research ethics concerns are apparent for the reported simulation and robotic manipulation experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is only moderate. The paper gives some implementation details, hardware, training schedule, and checkpoint sources, but the project/code link appears to be a placeholder or missing, and several details needed to reproduce the pruner architecture and baseline tuning are underspecified.

The real-world evidence is promising but small in scale. The paper reports three tasks with success percentages and frequencies, but does not clearly state trial counts in the main table, statistical uncertainty, or whether hyperparameters were selected on these tasks. Some real-world results are also mixed: SAG slightly reduces Stack Bowls success relative to full computation while improving Assembly Line substantially.

The central adaptivity claim is plausible but not fully isolated. The ablation replacing the pruner with a fixed schedule helps, but stronger controls would include learned fixed schedules, per-task oracle/static schedules, and comparisons under matched pruning masks or matched active block distributions.

The method requires training a task-specific pruner on representative reference data, even though the base diffusion policy is frozen. This somewhat weakens the framing of a lightweight or broadly deployable acceleration method, especially for new domains or distribution shifts.

The evaluation focuses on DP-T-style diffusion policies and relatively standard manipulation benchmarks. Generalization to larger VLA policies, different model architectures, longer-horizon tasks, and more diverse hardware remains an open question.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are minor issues: some claims such as 'without sacrificing performance' are slightly overstated given small degradations on several tasks, the project page is blank, and a few implementation/citation details look unfinished.
